Author: @Fs3i
Content:
The main benefit is the less air. When you’re flying an airplane, the main way you lose power is friction from the engine (super small), inefficient combustion (less small, still small overall), and moving air out of the way - that’s drag.

Most of the losses of the energy is just drag. If we have less drag, we need less engine, so the other two factors also get smaller.

You fly higher, you see less air. We’d always fly higher, but you’d need to push “too much” air down to stay flying at higher altitudes, so it’s less efficient again

Author: @TheEulerID
Content:
Most of the thrust from a modern turbofan jet engine does not come from the high speed exhaust gases, but from the giant fans which "bypass" the engine core. These high by-pass engines gain efficiency by accelerating a larger mass of air to relatively modest speeds, as it's more efficient. Hence the drive to bigger and bigger engines.

As for the effect of altitude then, true, there are fewer air molecules to create drag, but there are also fewer air molecules to divert downwards to generate lift. That's lift-induced drag, and means, all other things being equal, flying faster at higher altitude (although larger wings can counter-act some of this).

So, in general, the optimal altitude is strongly impacted by speed at which an aeroplane cruises at. Concorde flew considerably higher than subsonic jet airliners for that reason. In contrast, modern turboprops tend to fly slower and lower than "jet" airliners.

Correct me if im wrong but, I think I there’s a duality between fuel consumption and time. If I fly at the same thrust (force) as at a lower altitude, I’ll have a higher speed due to thinner air, so the flight time is shorter, but since the force over the same distance is the same, the total fuel consumption stays roughly equal.

On the other hand, if I fly at the same speed as at a lower altitude, I need less thrust because of the lower air resistance, which means less total work done and therefore less fuel consumption, but the travel time increases.

So basically, flying faster at higher altitude uses the same amount of fuel in contrary to what Veritasium says around halfway through the video.

Author: @wcubbin
Content:
The description risks confusing cause and effect with the point about the engines.
If air resistance was the only consideration we would fly outside the atmosphere where there is no resistance at all. But jet engines breathe air so there comes a point where there isn't enough air for them to produce enough thrust. Cruising altitude is a compromise between minimising drag, feeding enough air into the engines and finding favourable weather conditions. Also factored in is the cost of climbing to said altitude which is why short haul flights tend to fly lower.

Content:
Most of them are really just giant fans, they have a cold section up front that most of the thrust is produced from the forward fan blades. The ratio of the hot sections thrust to the cold sections use of energy is the bypass ratio. Meaning that the cold sections fan pushes more air in higher bypass systems. Turns out propellers are still what powers us and the most efficient jet motors are basically giant propellers driven directly by a jet engine that is not being used for jet propulsion but for a powerplant to turn the rotating forward props. 
Some engines ,like on fighter jets and higher speed uses, use hot gas as the primary force to provide the thrust. They have small or no fans up front that their primary focus is to compress gass to as dense as possible before fuel is sprayed. Once the fuel is compressed enough combustion is provided purely through pressure as jet fuel is more like kerosene or diesil fuel. And is combustible and not flammable... Author: @twentieth_r
Content: It's not that Jet Engines are more efficient at altitude, no combustion engines work better with LESS air. It's that they don't NEED to be as efficient at altitude, and thus, they can burn less fuel and consume less air because they're already at cruising speeds. A Jet Engine actually experiences starvation of o2 at higher altitudes, and that's why they adjust the fuel mixture on the fly - they produce more power and the pilot applies more thrust. They're not more efficient, they're actually far LESS efficient, they just don't require the efficiency because they've reached the altitude they'll fly at, keeping it there requires much less thrust.

Author: @Luciusf11
Content:
In terms of cruise efficiency in a piston powered airplane it can mathematically proven that altitude has no effect if you fly the exact same calibrated airspeed (CAS), ignoring the very slight differences in prop and engine efficiency. This is because identical CAS means identical drag and identical drag means identical thrust. Finally, power equals thrust times velocity making the power required rise with altitude in exact proportion to the increase in speed.

Since thrust and drag are equal to each other and constant with constant airspeed, HP = thrust (drag) * velocity (TAS), HP/TAS (and fuel/distance) required in cruise is invariant with altitude if the airspeed is constant assuming equal engine/prop efficiency.

We think that we're getting more nautical miles per gal (nmpg) at higher altitude because the air is thinner or because the true airspeed (TAS) for the same power is higher, but the reality is that we get more nmpg up high because our indicated airspeed (IAS) is lower on the same power.

What causes pilots to equate higher altitude with better fuel economy is that they usually compare nmpg at the same power (or lower power at the higher altitude) rather than at the same CAS. And since CAS drops with altitude if power is constant the efficiency goes up until you're high enough that CAS is down to best range speed.

TAS increases when you fly higher with the same power. But the cause of your nmpg increases is due to the fact that your CAS is closer to best glide speed Vbr.

When it comes recovering the energy lost in the climb, there are two components. One is the typical disparity between climb and descent airspeeds. Even if you were willing to slow down to climb speed on the way back to earth, your engine gets less efficient when producing very low power so you simply can't get it all back. Finally, during the climb to cruise altitude you are lifting fuel that won't be there when you descend and ironically the longer the trip the greater the effect of this. Fortunately, none of these issues has a significant effect on efficiency or range.

Author: @analyst-karanbabar
Content:
When air density drops at cruising altitude, an airplane must fly faster (roughly 73% faster) to maintain lift. While this boosts the engine's power requirement by the same factor (increasing fuel burned per hour), the higher speed also means covering distance quicker. Theoretically, this could result in similar total fuel consumption over a given distance.

However, real-world factors like engine efficiency at higher power settings and increased drag at very high speeds often lead to an overall increase in fuel consumption. Therefore, the primary benefits of flying higher are not always fuel savings, but rather reduced air traffic, smoother air, and faster trip times, which can indirectly save on crew salaries and maximize fixed asset (aircraft) utilization by completing more trips per day.

Author: @NoBeTyaaR
Content:
Planes fly at high altitudes—typically between 30,000 and 40,000 feet (9,000 to 12,000 meters)—for several key reasons:

1. Fuel Efficiency

At high altitudes, the air is thinner (lower density), which means there is less drag on the plane.

Less drag means the engines burn less fuel, making the flight more economical.


2. Weather Avoidance

Most weather systems, storms, and turbulence happen in the lower atmosphere (troposphere).

Flying higher helps aircraft avoid rough weather, making flights smoother and safer.


3. Air Traffic Separation

There's more vertical space at high altitudes to separate planes, reducing the risk of collisions and helping air traffic control manage routes more efficiently.


4. Engine Performance

Jet engines operate more efficiently at high altitudes where the temperature is lower and the air is less dense.


5. Emergency Options

Higher altitude gives pilots more time and space to deal with emergencies (like engine failure) by gliding to a safe landing area.

Author: @Mekkiceh
Content:
There is a mistake, I believe, about jet engines : They are not "more efficient at altitude" but they are optimized for the altitude the plane is flying at, because you can't make a jet engine that works good at every speed or every altitude so you have to choose in which flight domain you want them to work the best, then you work around it.

If for some reasons you wanted a jet engine more efficient at sea level (let say, a cruise missile that has to stay close to the ground to minimise interception), then you can make one.

The same thing happens with rocket engines, the nozzle design depends of the outside air pressure : an engine that works great at sea level, won't do good in the void of space (and the other way around). Which is one of the reasons why you have rocket stages, the weight of the extra engines compensating for the impossibility to make a unique one working great at every air pressure.

Author: @rewolff2
Content:
Everything before "not only that" is bogus. Not true. 
You have to think about the problem in a different way and gain an important insight. 
A glider has a glide ratio. Good gliders go 60 units forward for every 1 unit of altitude they lose. 
Now a powered airplane has a glide ratio too, somewhere in the 15-20 range. Flying straight and level means the engines have to provide exactly the energy needed to compensate for the altitude that would otherwise be lost. 
Applying this to a whole flight: To travel say 1000km from A to B with a plane with 20 glide ratio requires the engines to provide the energy to lift the plane 1000/20 = 50km. 
The glide ratio is quite independent on the air density: It depends on the shape of the plane with its wings. 
So independent of how high you fly, if you fly at the "best glide" speed, the amount of energy required will remain mostly the same. 
Two things make flying at 10-12km altitude attractive: First the engines are more efficient at that altitude. Secondly, you fly faster, so the plane can carry a new load of passengers more quickly.

Thats how evey commercial turbine works:

Normal commercial engines have timings (processes actually), first the turbine absorbs air molecules, then they are compressed, then compressed even further and sent to the chamber where little sprinklers sprinkle the fuel, then it is ignited and the byproduct gases give part of the thrust (20%)

However in jet engines, all of these processes happen at the same time and the thrust they produce is all it needs to fly at high speeds, which is also why they are more efficient at high altitudes such as those

And why only 20% in commercial engines you may ask? Bc there's an area around the turbine itself that lets the air through after being compressed once and that generates the other 80% of the thrust

Author: @tylerfb1
Content:
Here's why turbine engines get more efficient with altitude...to a point.:

There is a peculiar characteristic of turbine engines: the faster they spin for any thrust setting, the less fuel it takes to generate that thrust. Because of the lower density at altitude, for any given thrust setting, the engine speed will be higher. That increases their efficiency. 

Note: that does NOT mean they make more thrust at altitude. It means that for any given thrust, they burn less fuel.

Author: @tiemen9095
Content:
Its really very simple: in order to fly you need lift, equal to your weight. When generating lift, you generate drag and to compensate drag you need thrust. Thrust is related to fuel consumption per second.

So, ultimately in order to just keep flying we burn a certain amount of fuel every second. If we want to minimize fuel consumption we have to fly as fast as possible. However, flying faster increases our lift, so we need a way to decrease lift without increasing drag. Only way is to fly in less dense air. I.a.w. fly at high altitude. 

The argument that jet engines are more efficient if we fly higher, while true, is a bit awkward if you consider that at lower altitudes you would use propellers, which are more efficient than jets (more thrust per fuel flow). Jets are only more efficient because they still work when flyjng faster, and thus higher, which more than offsets the efficiency loss compared to propellers.

Author: @Quatuux
Content:
This explanation is WRONG. Or at least only partially true.

Jets could fly even higher and face even less air resistance but they don't do it. Why? Because the thermal efficiency of a jet engine is equal to 1-(temperature of outside air / temperature of combustion).
If you fly at a higher altitude, the temperature of the atmosphere increases so the thermal efficiency decreases and the fuel consumption increases.

Flying faster doesn't save fuel because you spend less time in the air.
Don't forget that the work produced by the engine is distance x force (thrust).

Flying higher doesn't necessarely require less thrust, but just allow to go faster without increasing thrust.
The faster the flight, the best it is for the company anyway, but not intrinsically by saving fuel.
